newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: ANC leader blames de Klerk for 1992 massacre.
newsitem.headline: ANC leader blames de Klerk for 1992 massacre.

text.p: Former South African president F.W. de Klerk's government was responsible for the 1992 "Bisho massacre" of 29 black protestors, African National Congress (ANC) leader Cyril Ramaphosa said on Monday.

Ramaphosa, secretary general of the ruling ANC, told Archbishop Desmond Tutu's Truth and Reconciliation Commission he believed a 60,000-strong crowd marching for the abolition of the Ciskei tribal homeland was lured into a trap.

Ramaphosa, now also one of the country's most influential black businessmen, said the gap in a border fence between South Africa and the nominally independent homeland, through which ANC marchers surged on September 7, 1992, had been cut deliberately.
"There was a trap...an ambush set for people who tried to move out of the stadium," he said.
The homeland army, which fired without warning, was led by Ciskei's then military ruler Brigadier Oupa Gqozo, but Ramaphosa said de Klerk's white government was ultimately to blame.

"The responsibility for the Bisho massacre rests squarely with the Ciskei regime and with the government of F.W. de Klerk, where the real power behind the Bisho government resided," he said. "Gqozo would not have had the courage to do what he did otherwise."

Recalling the incident, which rocked democracy talks between de Klerk's white government and Nelson Mandela's ANC, Tutu said: "It seemed as if we were entering a horrid night and the hopes for a settlement seemed to have been dashed."

Ramaphosa, then the ANC's chief democracy negotiator, was approaching homeland police and peace monitors at a razorwire barricade when shooting erupted close to the adjacent stadium in which ANC protestors were gathering.
Supporters and friends fell on top of Ramaphosa and other ANC leaders, but 29 people died and about 200 were wounded as soldiers continued to fire at the retreating crowd.
"I thought it lasted forever. There was terror and panic all around," Ramaphosa told the panel probing the human rights record of the last 30 years of white rule in South Africa.
"The saddest part was to see fairly elderly women dropping to the floor and crawling, to see the terror written on the faces of the young people."
Officials said Gqozo had not yet decided whether to give evidence at the three-day hearing, attended in wheelchairs by many surviving victims of the shooting.

But ANC activist Ronnie Kasrils, now deputy minister of defence, was to testify later on Monday about his decision to lead a charge from the stadium through the border gap towards the purpose-built capital a kilometre (mile) away.
Former foreign minister Pik Botha was also expected to give evidence to the commission, which can pardon politically motivated human rights offences and compensate victims.
